messages.body_plain:
Hi Wessel,
I restructured your code a bit, have a look at it. Is this what you are trying to achieve?

Best,
Bart

library(simmer)

env <- simmer()

my_function <- function(attrs){
  time <- attrs['start_time']
  if(time < 5){
    print("small time")
  } else{
    print("big time")
  }

  return(0) # timeout will be of duration 0

}

patient <-
  trajectory("patient's path") %>%
  log_("Here I am") %>%
  set_attribute("start_time", function() {now(env)}) %>%

  timeout(my_function)

env %>%
  add_generator("patient", patient, at(seq(0,10,1))) %>%
  run()

I'm not sure I understand what exactly you want to accomplish, but:

If you need to follow different sub-trajectories based on certain
conditions, then you need the branch() activity. You'll find several
examples in the vignettes. If you need one path, without forks, but
you want modularity and reuse, you can define parts of the trajectory
and then concatenate them with join(). If you want to stop at some
point (for instance, run path1 but not path2 if some condition holds),
you need to place the leave() activity between path1 and path2.

Iñaki

simmer's golden rule: one activity, one action; and vice versa. You
cannot wait some time OR follow another path in the same activity. You
have to break down your actions and put them into different
activities. For example:

my_function <- function(){
  time <- get_attribute(env, start_time)
  if(time < 5){

     return(1) # we want the trajectory to wait small time
  } else{
    return(2) # we want to join a new trajectory
}

my_trajectory <- trajectory() %>%
  ...
  branch(my_function, continue=c(T, F), # or whatever
              # option 1
              timeout(function() get_attribute(env, "start_time")),
              # option 2

messages.subject_clean: simmer.optim - how to pass parameters to a function to be optmized
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have already created a simmer model to simulate a facility. It works well and I have also succeeded to optimizing the number of users.

Now I would like to optimize the budget to be spent with each type of facility, meaning that the simmer will feed a function that calculates the costs of each facility.

Being so, I have built my optimization object like below:

optimRes <- simmer_optim(
  model = SimModel,
  method = sa_optim,
  direction = "min",
  objective = OptimVpl,
  constraints = list(with_args(assert_waiting_time_max, max_val = 60)),
  params = list(runTime = par_discrete(20:60),
                facility1 = par_discrete(4:20),
                facility2 = par_discrete(20:80),
                facility3 = par_discrete(50:200)),
  control = optim_control(run_args = list(until = runTimeMax),
                          sa_optim = list(maxit = 5),
                          parallel = TRUE)
)

The objective function is OptimVpl and it requires the information regarding the params and environment to correctly allocate the facilities costs.

I would like to know how to pass parameters and environment to the function to be optimized?

Thanks for your help.

2017-09-21 20:22 GMT+02:00 RgrNormand <r...@ynro.eu>:
> The objective function is OptimVpl and it requires the information regarding
> the params and environment to correctly allocate the facilities costs.
>
> I would like to know how to pass parameters and environment to the function
> to be optimized?

Sorry, there is a lack of documentation about this, because
simmer.optim is still in alpha version.

The prototype for your optimisation function should be something like this:

OptimVpl <- function(envs) { ... }

Optionally, you can define more arguments, but you will always receive
the output from the simulation model (the simmer environment or
environments) as first argument. From that environment(s) you can
extract all the information you need (using
get_mon_arrivals/attributes/resources) to compute the costs.

Regards,
Iñaki

You are right: it shouldn't happen, thanks for the report!

> In order to get the simulation values I am using msr_resource_capacity. Is
> this approach ok?

The msr_* functions are helpers for measuring things, and of course
you can use them inside your custom objective. We didn't think about
them a lot yet, so use them with caution and reading the code, which
is here: https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer.optim/blob/master/R/measures.R

As you'll see, msr_resource_capacity simply returns the mean capacity
of a resource at the end of the simulation. If you need this, then
it's ok.

>
> get_mon_arrivals(envs) %>%
>   filter(end_time < 4*60) %>%
>   mutate(waiting_time = end_time - start_time ) %>%
>   .$waiting_time

Unfortunately not yet. As I said, we haven't given these helpers much
thought yet, but eventually we'll provide this kind of common
measures. For the moment, you can wrap that code into a function and
reuse it in your optimisations.

> Another point would be to run the optimization, at least for the grid

> implemented in parallel (and I am using it), but I believe the search itself
> could benefit from more cores. In my particular case, SA and DE options are
> not reaching the best results (I understand that both methods can't
> guarantee that).

That's a very good point. I'm going to open an issue right away,
because I believe that simmer.optim should support parallel
optimisation whenever it's possible with minimum pain from the user
side.

> I was wondering that perhaps complex models could have a previous check of
> some simpler conditions prior to run the full optimization function. E.g.:
> if the max waiting time condition is not satisfied, there is no point in
> running that function.

Agree: whenever it's possible to determine that a condition is not,
and will not be, satisfied, the simulation should stop right away and
throw an error. We'll look into it.

> anyway. I am not that skilled but have faced few interesting challenges in
> the past. If possible, let me know.

You are doing it! Of course new code is always welcome, but this kind
of contribution is very helpful: please keep reporting your
experiences, needs, problems... what is missing, what can be
improved... either on Github or here as you are already doing. Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi,I am starting to use SIMMER. My question might not be very difficult but still please help me out. I have 2 types of arrivals fighting for the same resource. I tried plotting the total queue length using simmer.plot which is working. But how do I plot total number of each arrival type in the queue over the entire time period? Is there any elegant way?

Example : At a ticket counter there are males and females arriving at a different rate. I am able to plot the total queue length. But how to I plot the total number of males and females in the queue seperately?

Thanks

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

2017-09-26 23:19 GMT+02:00 salman anis <1reach...@gmail.com>:

> Hi,I am starting to use SIMMER. My question might not be very difficult but still please help me out. I have 2 types of arrivals fighting for the same resource. I tried plotting the total queue length using simmer.plot which is working. But how do I plot total number of each arrival type in the queue over the entire time period? Is there any elegant way?
>
> Example : At a ticket counter there are males and females arriving at a different rate. I am able to plot the total queue length. But how to I plot the total number of males and females in the queue seperately?

You can use additional “dumb” resources to account for that. Example:
library(simmer)
library(simmer.plot)

person <- function(sex, lambda)
  trajectory() %>%
  seize(sex) %>%
  seize("counter") %>%
  release(sex) %>%
  timeout(function() rexp(1, lambda)) %>%
  release("counter")

env <- simmer() %>%
  add_resource("counter", 1, Inf) %>%
  add_resource("male", Inf, 0) %>%
  add_generator("male", person("male", 2), function() rexp(100, 1)) %>%
  add_resource("female", Inf, 0) %>%
  add_generator("female", person("female", 3), function() rexp(100, 1)) %>%
  run(1000)

plot(env, "resources", "usage", c("male", "female", "counter"))

Regards,
Iñaki
​
